extracted.intended_audience: student reporters and newspaper journalists (reporters learning news-writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting political news (especially elections—forecasts, election-day coverage, returns) and labor troubles/strikes, showing what facts, perspectives, and human details to include. Focused toward reporters preparing news stories for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of election stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Three common kinds of election stories are: (1) an analysis of political conditions preceding an election with or without a forecast of the result, (2) a description of election day conditions and events, (3) the results of the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to choose story approach; examples in the text illustrate each kind (political forecast, election-day narrative, and return/summary pieces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial presentation of political news
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some newspapers are sufficiently independent in politics to treat political news without partisan bias, many papers still present such news from the point of view of their editorial policy. There is a growing tendency, however, to present both sides fairly in news columns and to confine partisanship to editorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News stories should aim to present both sides fairly; reserve explicit partisanship for opinion/editorial pages. Balance and fairness are emphasized as evolving professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election return story elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Election return stories consist largely of summaries of the most important results of the election, such as: (1) the candidates elected and defeated, (2) the majority or plurality of the successful candidates, (3) the effect of the election on the political complexion of legislative bodies, (4) causes of victory and defeat, (5) statements by candidates and party managers in regard to the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these specific factual items in return pieces; support with quoted statements from candidates/party leaders and contextual analysis of legislative/political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political forecast reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Forecasts should analyze political conditions preceding an election and may predict results based on investigation and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base forecasts on informed local canvassing, check lists, comparisons with prior elections, and reasoned arguments about defections and party strength (as in the Springfield Republican example). Explain the basis for predictions rather than making unsupported claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-day coverage: turnout, timing, and voting mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report conditions affecting voting on election day: weather, ballot design and its effect on speed/confusion, turnout patterns (early voting percentages, lulls, rush hours), and timing observations (percent of vote by noon, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistics (percentages, times), observed pacing (e.g., 'nearly half the votes were cast by 9 o'clock'), and note any innovations (modified ballots, sample ballots) that affected voting speed and voter behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-day coverage: polling-place incidents and safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Document polling-place disputes, challenges, arrests or near-arrests, board composition (inspectors present), searches for fraud, special inspectors/deputies sent out, and legal compliance issues when they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give specifics (locations, names, duration—e.g., a 17-minute argument that stopped voting), and note official responses (sending special inspectors, Deputies), as these are important to readers' understanding of election integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-day coverage: voter education and observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on voter education efforts (sample ballots, instructors) and the activities of watchers/volunteer observers (e.g., Honest Ballot Association squads, Volunteer Watchers' League, notable volunteer groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how parties or civic groups assisted voters or monitored polls; include notable human-interest details (e.g., former football stars serving as watchers) to give color and illustrate civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include advocacy and campaign-group activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover the activities of advocacy organizations at polling places (distributing literature, staffing headquarters, notable leaders present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name organizations, their leaders, and describe distribution and presence (times and places) — e.g., Women's Political Union distributing suffrage literature and leaders staffing districts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and accurate presentation in labor stories
rubrics_metrics.description: A fair and accurate presentation of the points of view of both the employers and the employees is essential in all stories of this kind. Statements from both sides, therefore, are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always seek and include comment from management and labor leaders; balance direct quotes and formal statements with on-the-ground accounts from workers and employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest and living/working conditions in strike coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Although stories in this class are largely informative, there is also a chance for human interest treatment. Accounts of living and working conditions, for example, as obtained from workmen and their families often give a better picture of the circumstances that produced the strike than do formal statements by labor leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews with workers and families to show conditions; such humanizing detail can explain causes and evoke legitimate sympathy when appropriate (especially when strikers 'are in actual want').

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike-story components: demands, negotiations, scope, and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike reports should set out the union's demands (wage increases, hours, seniority rights, representation), negotiation history (offers, arbitration proposals), numbers affected (employees, miles of railroad, companies), and possible or actual economic and service impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete figures (number of men, miles of railroad, percent/amount of proposed wage increases), list the employers/companies involved, summarize offers and refusals (arbitration under statutes like the Erdman Act where relevant), and explain wider consequences (tie-ups, displaced employees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete economic detail to illustrate grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: Give specific numeric examples of pay and expenses to illustrate the workers' economic position (for example, the taxi driver who took home $7 after expenses because of a 20% split and gasoline/maintenance costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down wage proposals and typical week earnings/expenses to let readers judge the reasonableness of demands; such detail strengthens the story's explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive journalism: furnish facts for intelligent understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the settlement of labor troubles not infrequently is brought about by the influence of public opinion, constructive journalism recognizes the importance of furnishing readers with all of the facts necessary for an intelligent understanding of the issues and conditions involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond mere narrative, provide context, background, data, and perspectives that help readers form informed opinions; avoid sensationalism that obscures the substantive issues.
